JSON: Name: cleavenet_pipeline Title: Deep-learning-guided conditional generation and prediction of peptide substrates to design efficient and selective protease substrates Short Hypothesis: A combined deep-learning pipeline that (1) predicts continuous multi-protease cleavage scores from peptide sequence and (2) conditionally generates peptide sequences conditioned on desired cleavage profiles will produce synthetic 10-mer substrates that exhibit higher in vitro cleavage efficiency and/or greater selectivity for a target protease (e.g., MMP13) than substrates sampled from position-wise amino-acid distributions or existing literature-derived substrates. Related Work: Existing approaches to protease substrate design include: (a) experimental high-throughput display and phage/ribosome/mRNA libraries which produce large labeled datasets but are costly and assay-specific; (b) substitution-matrix and motif-based methods that capture position-wise preferences but ignore inter-residue cooperativity and return limited ranking power; (c) structure- and docking-based methods that can explain interactions but are computationally expensive and limited by structural availability and scoring inaccuracies; and (d) supervised classifiers for cleavage-site prediction that typically output binary labels and cannot rank continuous cleavage efficiency or condition generation. Generative protein design methods from language-models and diffusion models have shown capability to produce functional sequences but have been applied incompletely to protease substrates and rarely incorporate multi-output, continuous activity conditioning. Key limitations across prior methods are lack of continuous multi-protease scoring, inability to condition generation on a desired cleavage profile (efficiency and selectivity), limited capture of subsite cooperativity, and insufficient experimental calibration across assay modalities. Abstract: We propose an end-to-end deep-learning pipeline for protease substrate design that couples a multi-output cleavage-score predictor with a conditional autoregressive peptide generator. The predictor maps peptide sequences to continuous cleavage scores across a set of proteases and provides uncertainty estimates via an ensemble. The generator produces variable-length peptides either unconditionally or conditioned on a target multi-protease cleavage profile (efficiency and selectivity). Applied to matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), the pipeline is trained on a large mRNA-display peptide dataset and validated on independent fluorescence-based assays and in vitro screening of recombinant proteases. Main contributions are: (1) a continuous multi-protease scoring model that generalizes across assay modalities; (2) a conditioning mechanism that steers generation toward substrates with defined efficiency/selectivity profiles; and (3) experimental validation showing generated peptides that outperform position-wise baselines in efficiency and yield peptides with MMP13-selective cleavage not present in training. Expected outcomes include reproducible in silico nomination of candidate substrates, calibrated cleavage-score thresholds linked to in vitro outcomes, and a framework extensible to other protease families. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Training/validation: mRNA-display dataset of 18,583 10-mer peptides with normalized continuous Z cleavage scores across 18 MMPs; perform an 80/20 train/test split and remove test sequences with Levenshtein distance <3 to any training sequence to produce a homology-filtered test set (~2,901 sequences). (2) Out-of-distribution test: independent fluorescence FRET dataset (71 peptides) assayed against seven recombinant MMPs. (3) Experimental validation: synthesize FRET-paired panels of peptides: (a) 24 top-ranked MMP13-efficiency candidates from unconditional generation; (b) 24 top-ranked MMP13-selectivity candidates from conditional generation; (c) baseline groups: 8 site-independent (position-wise sampled) sequences, 8 site-independent sequences re-ranked by the predictor, and 15 control sequences from the mRNA-display training set (positive and negative controls). In vitro assays: measure cleavage (fluorescence increase) for the 95-peptide panel against 12 available recombinant MMPs under standardized buffer and temperature conditions, duplicate technical runs with independent protease preps. Models and baselines: (A) Predictor: compare bidirectional LSTM and transformer multi-output regressors (ensemble of 5 for uncertainty) against a site-independent baseline that uses position-wise amino-acid frequencies. (B) Generator: autoregressive decoder-only transformer trained both unconditionally and conditionally (conditioning vector = rounded Z-scores across 18 MMPs). Evaluation metrics: Pearson correlation (r) and MAE between predicted and true continuous Z-scores on test sets; ROC-AUC across a range of cleavage thresholds for binary classification; calibration metrics (expected vs empirical MAE vs model uncertainty), hit-rate (fraction of synthesized peptides with measurable in vitro cleavage), fold-change and normalized cleavage efficiency (0-1 mapping), selectivity score S = normalized target cleavage relative to others, and clustering-based concordance with protease phylogeny. Ablations and comparisons: (1) architecture ablation: transformer vs LSTM predictor and generator; (2) uncertainty ablation: ensemble predictor vs single model; (3) generation ablation: conditional vs unconditional generator; (4) baseline comparison: generated sequences vs site-independent position-wise samples vs top training substrates; (5) dataset-robustness: train on reduced fractions (50%, 25%) to measure performance degradation. Statistical tests: report Pearson r with 95% CI, MAE mean±s.d., ROC-AUC with CI, Kruskal–Wallis for group differences, and report exact p-values. Reporting: compute MMP-specific predicted-to-empirical cleavage thresholds (maximize ROC-AUC) and apply to corrected efficiency and selectivity analyses. Risk Factors and Limitations: Data and assay biases: mRNA-display-derived Z-scores and fluorescence FRET assays differ in length distribution, chemical context, and dynamic range; model trained on display data may not generalize to all in vitro or in vivo contexts. Label noise and threshold ambiguity: continuous Z-scores are assay-dependent and may not map linearly to absolute cleavage rates; inferred cleavage thresholds can be dataset-specific. Model failure modes: memorization of training sequences, mode collapse or low diversity in generator outputs, and overfitting to dominant motifs reduce novelty. Limited sequence space coverage: short peptide models cannot capture post-translational modifications or long-range structural context present in full-length natural substrates. Selectivity ceiling: closely related proteases with overlapping specificity (e.g., MMP family) may impose an upper bound on achievable selectivity; predicted selectivity may not hold in complex biological fluids. Computational constraints: training ensembles and large autoregressive transformers requires substantial GPU resources and may limit iterative design. Domain transfer: extension to non-MMP proteases, non-natural amino acids, or cellular/in vivo cleavage predictions requires new datasets and retraining; current pipeline is validated only on synthetic peptide substrates and recombinant proteases.
